title: The same write delivered twice at the same time

R1.reason: Idempotency-Key per user action, reused on retry, UNIQUE(user_id, idempotency_key) in Postgres. But there is no payload fingerprint, and the key is not scoped by operation or tenant.

R2.reason: The redemption claim, cap update and ledger credit all run in one transaction. A concurrent duplicate blocks on the unique index and then replays on commit. The database handles the concurrency.

R3.reason: There is no same-key, different-payload check. The 409 is only for a different key on the same user and voucher. A reused key with a different voucher code would just insert a new row and hit the key unique constraint, and the handler's recovery path does not cover that.

R4.reason: UNIQUE(voucher_id, user_id) on redemptions is the primary guard. UNIQUE(ref_type, ref_id) on the ledger is a third.

R5.reason: It proposes a concurrency test with 20 parallel calls, same key and different keys, asserting one ledger row. It does not say the test should run against real PostgreSQL.

forbidden.item: In-memory deduplication or a Redis TTL key as the only guard
forbidden.evidence: It says an in-memory or Redis-only guard should be avoided and uses database constraints.

forbidden.item: Check then insert without a unique constraint
forbidden.evidence: It warns that a SELECT-then-credit check races and uses unique constraints.

forbidden.item: Relying on a queue job id for uniqueness
Telling the client to generate a new key on retry
forbidden.evidence: It says to reuse the same key on every retry. A new key is suggested only for a genuinely new user attempt.

grade.summary: It is a sound database-constraint design with an atomic transaction and a business unique guard. It lacks a payload fingerprint and same-key-different-payload 409 handling, and its test plan does not name real PostgreSQL.
